clue.text: Fluttering leaf? As if! Sure!

indicators.note: something fluttering flaps about restlessly, so the letters that follow are thrown into a new order

parts.note: the letters of these words, ignoring punctuation

explanation.surface: Someone scoffs at the idea of a falling leaf, sarcastically exclaiming 'As if! Sure!'
explanation.walkthrough: The exclamations read as sarcasm, but 'Sure' is a straight definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A failsafe system is designed so it cannot go wrong, making it certain and reliable.

clue.text: Geological evidence from UFOs? Silly

indicators.note: the letters are taken out of the run of words that follows, straddling the gap between them

parts.note: found inside the two words once the punctuation is ignored

explanation.surface: A sceptic mocks the idea that flying saucers have left any evidence in the rocks.
explanation.definitionFit: Preserved remains of ancient life in rock strata are the evidence geologists use to date layers.

clue.text: Regularly seen in mist, tall birch tilting

indicators.note: regularly means at even intervals, so every second letter of the following words is kept

parts.note: the second, fourth, sixth letters and so on

explanation.surface: A tall birch tree leans over, glimpsed through the mist.
explanation.definitionFit: Italic type slopes to the right, so sloping or slanted lettering is what the word describes.

clue.text: University rejected movement of 'phony music' like Beethoven's 5th

indicators.note: a movement shifts things about, so the letters are moved into a new order
what is rejected is thrown out, so that letter is removed from the fodder

parts.note: U is the standard abbreviation for university
the letters of the quoted phrase

explanation.surface: A university rejects a modern composition as fake music, unlike a Beethoven classic.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Movement' looks like a musical term in this surface, but it signals the letters moving.
explanation.definitionFit: Beethoven's Fifth is a symphony, so anything resembling it is of that orchestral form.

clue.text: Move one lorry of bananas at any cost

indicators.note: going bananas means going crazy, so the letters run wild into another order

parts.note: the letters of these four words

explanation.surface: A haulier is told to shift a lorry full of bananas whatever it takes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Of bananas' reads as the lorry's cargo, but 'of' is fodder and 'bananas' means mad.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom means a thing will not happen under any circumstances, whatever price or inducement is offered.

clue.text: Subject is suppressing resistance ring

indicators.note: to suppress something is to hold it down within, so one word encloses the other

parts.note: a subject of discussion
R is the symbol for electrical resistance

explanation.surface: A subject in some trial or experiment is holding back a group's resistance.
explanation.definitionFit: Each tropic is a circle of latitude drawn round the globe, so a ring around the Earth.

clue.text: Auntie's known for this: some flipping rheumatoid arthritis

indicators.note: flipping something turns it over, so the run of letters is read backwards
only some of the letters of the following phrase are used, a run sitting inside it

parts.note: the end of the first word and the start of the second

explanation.surface: An elderly aunt is famous for her flare-ups of rheumatoid arthritis.
explanation.walkthrough: Auntie, or Auntie Beeb, is a British nickname for the BBC, which began as a broadcaster on the wireless.
explanation.definitionFit: The BBC made its name with wireless broadcasting before television, so the nickname is tied to that medium.

clue.text: Quiet about struggles to include Western trailers

indicators.note: to include something is to take it inside, so one piece goes within another

parts.note: p, piano, is the musical direction for quiet
re means about or concerning
competes or struggles
W is the abbreviation for Western

explanation.surface: A film-maker quietly worries about the difficulty of cramming a Western into the coming attractions.
explanation.definitionFit: Trailers are short advance showings of films, screened before release to advertise them.

clue.text: Brief agreement written up, son's respectful gestures

parts.note: curt means short or brief

indicators.note: in a down entry, writing a word upwards means its letters run from bottom to top

parts.note: a word of agreement
S is the abbreviation for son

explanation.surface: A short deal is recorded, and a son makes polite gestures of thanks.
explanation.definitionFit: A curtsy is a bob made by bending the knees, a traditional sign of respect to royalty.

clue.text: Like Bugs when bugged?

parts.note: surface reading: how a creature behaves when insects or listening devices trouble it
setter's reading: the cartoon rabbit Bugs, when annoyed, would be described by a slang phrase for a disgruntled person

explanation.walkthrough: Bugs is Bugs Bunny, and bugged means irritated; the phrase is slang for someone fed up.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom describes an annoyed or displeased person, and literally fits an irritated cartoon rabbit.

clue.text: Conman not about to get left in prison

indicators.note: not marks a letter that must be taken out of the word before it
to get means to receive something in its place, so a new letter fills the gap

parts.note: a swindler
c, circa, means about
L is the abbreviation for left

explanation.surface: A conman, no longer around, has been abandoned in jail.
explanation.walkthrough: The C of circa in the swindler's name is swapped for L.
explanation.definitionFit: Slammer is slang for a jail, from the sound of cell doors banging shut.

clue.text: Pensioner disrespectfully told 'not to start reckless dare'

indicators.note: not starting means the opening letter is dropped

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: something reckless is wild and disordered, so the letters are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: An elderly person is rudely warned against taking up a foolhardy challenge.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Told' looks like the verb of the sentence, but it is fodder that loses its first letter.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase is a patronising, mildly rude name for an elderly woman drawing a state pension.

clue.text: Rishi's reconstruction — people allegedly lucky

indicators.note: a reconstruction rebuilds something in a new form, so the letters are reassembled

parts.note: the letters of the name

explanation.surface: Rishi Sunak's rebuilding project relies on supposedly fortunate voters.
explanation.walkthrough: Rishi Sunak was a UK prime minister.
explanation.definitionFit: The saying 'the luck of the Irish' credits that nation with proverbial good fortune.

clue.text: We're told, alternatively, a conservative has debts or works

parts.note: or introduces an alternative

indicators.note: being told something means hearing it spoken, so the result is judged by sound

parts.note: a, plus Tory for a Conservative, plus IOUs for debts

explanation.surface: A rumour goes round that a Tory politician has either debts or a job.
explanation.walkthrough: IOUs are written promises to pay, so debts; said quickly, the string sounds like the musical works.
explanation.definitionFit: Oratorios are large-scale musical compositions for voices and orchestra, typically on sacred themes, by Handel and others.

clue.text: Actor in Shakespeare's Trouble and Strife

definitions.meaning: first meaning: a Hollywood film star
second meaning: the playwright's spouse, using rhyming slang

explanation.walkthrough: Trouble and strife is Cockney rhyming slang for wife; the clue reads like an actor appearing in an unknown Shakespeare play.
explanation.definitionFit: An American film star shares her name with the woman William Shakespeare married in 1582.

clue.text: Walking in fog, lost, going after love, wearing belt

indicators.note: something worn goes around the wearer, so the outer piece encloses the rest

parts.note: to belt is to strike or hit

indicators.note: going after means following, so one piece is placed behind the other

parts.note: love is zero in tennis, shaped like O

indicators.note: being lost means wandering astray, so the letters go astray into a new order

parts.note: the letters of these two words

explanation.surface: Someone lost in the fog wanders after a sweetheart, wearing a belt.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Wearing belt' sounds like clothing, but the word for belt goes around the other pieces, split across both ends.
explanation.definitionFit: Hoofing it is informal for travelling on foot, using one's hooves as it were.

clue.text: Excuses given by European missing in attacks

parts.note: E is the abbreviation for European

indicators.note: something missing is absent, so those letters are taken away

parts.note: taken as written
military incursions

explanation.surface: A European soldier absent from the assaults offers pretexts.
explanation.definitionFit: Evasions are dodges or ways of avoiding the truth, much like excuses offered in place of answers.

clue.text: Spies ill prepared …

indicators.note: prepared means made ready or worked up, so the letters are worked into another form

parts.note: the letters of these two words

explanation.surface: Secret agents are badly prepared, and the sentence trails off ominously.
explanation.walkthrough: The three dots look like mere punctuation for suspense, but they are the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: The three dots marking an omission or trailing thought are called by this punctuation name.

clue.text: Unlikely apricot-lover?

indicators.note: unlikely suggests something improbable or out of place, so the letters are set in an unexpected order

parts.note: the letters of the compound, ignoring the hyphen

explanation.surface: Who would hardly be a fan of soft fruit?
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue is also the definition: a meat-eating dinosaur is an improbable fruit lover.
explanation.definitionFit: This carnivorous predatory dinosaur hunted prey, so it would be about the last creature to crave fruit.

clue.text: Dog holding tune, Come Together

indicators.note: holding something means having it within one's grasp, so one word surrounds the other

parts.note: a young dog
an air is a melody

explanation.surface: A dog clings to a Beatles tune, Come Together.
explanation.walkthrough: Come Together is a Beatles song, which makes the capitals look like a title rather than a definition.
explanation.definitionFit: To form a couple or team is to join up with a partner, uniting as two.

clue.text: Vicar gets electronic kit to modernize

parts.note: Rev, Reverend, is a vicar's title
an amplifier, a piece of electronic equipment

explanation.surface: A vicar buys an amplifier to bring the church services up to date.
explanation.definitionFit: To revamp something is to renovate it and give it a new, updated appearance.

clue.text: Furore with turkey as practical joke

parts.note: kicking up a stink is causing an uproar
a turkey is a flop, and a flop bombs

explanation.surface: There is uproar over a turkey that turned out to be a prank.
explanation.definitionFit: A small device releasing a foul smell is a classic prankster's trick, so a jokey stunt.

clue.text: Somewhere in church, reported villainous character

indicators.note: a report is spoken aloud, so the word is judged by how it sounds

parts.note: the nave is the main body of a church

explanation.surface: A wicked figure has been seen somewhere inside a church.
explanation.walkthrough: The silent K means the place in church and the rogue sound identical.
explanation.definitionFit: A knave is an old word for a dishonest rogue or scoundrel, also the jack in cards.

clue.text: Everyman, rank and fuming

parts.note: the setter refers to himself as I
to rank is to rate

explanation.surface: The setter is foul-smelling and furious.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rank' wants to mean smelly, and fuming seems to agree; it is the verb meaning to grade.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone fuming is seething with anger, which is to be very angry indeed.

clue.text: Performing male's accepted by Everyman formally

indicators.note: something accepted is taken in, so it sits within the other word

parts.note: one is the formal impersonal pronoun for anybody, every man
a stag is an adult male deer

explanation.surface: A man's acting is formally approved by the setter.
explanation.definitionFit: Being on the stage means appearing before an audience, in the middle of a show.

clue.text: Frightful migraine, head splitting somewhere in Africa

indicators.note: frightful suggests a dreadful mess, so the letters are scrambled
the head splitting off means the first letter breaks away and is dropped

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone suffers a dreadful migraine with a splitting head while travelling in Africa.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Head splitting' looks like the headache's symptom, but it removes the first letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Nigeria is a West African country, so it is one particular place on that continent.

clue.text: South American congress assembled ancient kingdom

parts.note: S is the abbreviation for south
US, the United States, stands for American
congress in its sense of sexual intercourse

explanation.surface: A South American legislature has gathered in an old realm.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Congress' looks like a parliament beside 'American'; it is the old word for intercourse. SUSSEX is an English county that was once an Anglo-Saxon kingdom.
explanation.definitionFit: The South Saxons formed a kingdom in early medieval England before it was absorbed into Wessex.

clue.text: Primarily, style Yazoo notably tried, having plenty of pep?

definitions.text: style Yazoo notably tried, having plenty of pep

indicators.note: primarily means first of all, so only the opening letter of each word is kept

parts.words: style Yazoo notably tried, having plenty of pep
parts.note: the initial of each of these eight words

explanation.surface: A music writer describes a lively genre the band Yazoo famously experimented with.
explanation.walkthrough: Yazoo was an English 1980s electronic duo of Vince Clarke and Alison Moyet, so the whole clue also defines the genre.
explanation.definitionFit: Synth-pop is upbeat 1980s pop music built on synthesizers, the very style that Yazoo played.
